definition: A comparison of a player's recent workload (usually one week) with their longer-term average (usually four weeks). Used to flag sudden spikes in load, though its use as a single decision-making number is debated.
Predicting what a delivery will do before or shortly after release, using cues from the bowler's body and the ball's early flight.
The moment in the bowling action when the back foot lands after the bound. Hip and shoulder alignment here is used to classify action types.
Spin in which the bottom of the ball moves forward. It produces an upward Magnus force in flight and tends to make the ball skid on after bouncing.
A camera-based system that locates the ball in three dimensions, reconstructs its path and, for LBW reviews, predicts where it would have gone after hitting the batter.
The thin layer of air next to the ball's surface, slowed by friction. Whether it is laminar or turbulent controls where the airflow separates — the basis of swing.
The final leap of a fast bowler's run-up before delivery, also called the pre-delivery stride.
How far and how high a ball travels after bouncing before reaching the wicket-keeper, or how far a hit ball travels in the air.
The point on a bat where an impact produces almost no sideways jolt at the handle. It sits close to the sweet spot.
Performing worse than one's normal skill level because of pressure.
A device that drops a weight onto a surface and measures how sharply it decelerates. Used to measure pitch hardness, which predicts bounce.
The ratio of rebound speed to approach speed in a collision. A higher value means a bouncier collision, whether ball on pitch or ball on bat.
Sideways movement in the air towards the direction the seam points, caused by a laminar boundary layer on one side and a turbulent one on the other.
In a bowling action, the shoulders twisting back towards side-on against the hips during the delivery stride. Long blamed for lower-back injury, though a 2021 prospective study did not single it out.
A pace bowler's delivery in which the fingers drag across the ball at release to impart some spin and take off pace, so it grips and deviates off the pitch.
Water that condenses on the grass when it cools below the dew point, usually after sunset. Makes the ball wet and harder to grip.
A spinning ball dropping faster than gravity alone would make it, caused by top-spin and the Magnus force.
The change in frequency of a wave reflected from a moving object. Radar speed guns use it to measure ball speed.
The air's resistance to the ball's motion. It grows with the square of speed and slows a fast delivery by roughly 15–18 km/h before it reaches the batter.
A number describing how much drag a shape produces for its size. Roughly 0.4–0.5 for a cricket ball.
Sideways curve of a spinning ball in the air before it bounces, caused by the Magnus force. Different from turn, which happens off the pitch.
The Decision Review System, which lets teams challenge on-field decisions using ball-tracking, edge detection and replays.
Technology for deciding whether the ball touched the bat, using stump-microphone audio synced to video, or infrared heat cameras.
Straightening of the elbow. In bowling, extension of more than 15° during the delivery swing, measured in testing, makes an action illegal under ICC regulations.
A cultivated variety of white willow used for professional bats because it is light, tough and springy.
Rough patches on the pitch made by bowlers' follow-throughs. Spinners aim at them because the ball grips and bounces unpredictably.
The moment the bowler's front foot lands. Ground reaction forces here are several times body weight, and a braced front leg is linked with higher pace.
The force the ground pushes back on the body with when a foot lands. Measured with force plates in biomechanics labs.
In an LBW review, the space between the outer edges of off and leg stump, from the ground upward, where the ball must strike the batter.
Cameras that show heat. In reviews, used to spot small warm marks left by friction when the ball touches bat or glove.
The sequence in which body segments speed up one after another — legs, hips, trunk, shoulder, arm, hand — to create a fast movement at the end of the chain.
Repeatedly tapping a new bat's face with a mallet or old ball to compress the wood fibres so it can take hard impacts without cracking.
Smooth, orderly airflow in layers. A laminar boundary layer separates from the ball relatively early.
Leg before wicket: a batter can be out if the ball would have hit the stumps but was intercepted by the body, subject to rules about where it pitched and struck.
A fatigue crack in a vertebra of the lower back, caused by repeated loading. A well-documented injury in young fast bowlers.
The sideways force on a spinning ball moving through air. Causes drift and dip in spin bowling.

A bowling action in which the hips and shoulders are misaligned, with the shoulders counter-rotating against the hips. Long linked to back injury; newer research points more to pelvis and lower-back control.
A research method that hides part of a scene (spatial) or cuts it off at a moment in time (temporal) to test what information players use to anticipate.
The internal stitched join between the two leather pieces on each half of a four-piece ball, running at right angles to the main seam.
Swing away from the direction the seam points, which happens when both sides of the ball have turbulent boundary layers — usually with an old, roughened ball.
A dimensionless number, speed × diameter ÷ kinematic viscosity, that indicates whether flow around the ball is likely to be laminar or turbulent.
A rapid jump of the eyes from one point to another. Batters make predictive saccades ahead of the ball to around the bounce point.
The raised line of stitching joining the two halves of the ball. It trips the airflow for swing and grips the pitch for seam movement.
Sideways deviation off the pitch when the ball lands on its seam. Different from swing, which happens in the air.
Where the boundary layer leaves the ball's surface. Different separation points on the two sides create the sideways force behind swing.
The zone on a bat's blade where impacts lose the least energy to vibration, so the ball leaves fastest with little sting in the hands.
The speed at which drag on a falling object equals its weight, so it stops accelerating. Roughly 130–145 km/h for a cricket ball.
Spin in which the top of the ball moves forward. It makes the ball dip in flight and kick up off the pitch.
Working out a point's position in 3D from its position in two or more camera views taken from different angles.
Chaotic, mixing airflow. A turbulent boundary layer stays attached to the ball further round than a laminar one.
The change in direction of a spinning ball when it grips the pitch at the bounce.
A DRS outcome in which the tracked ball is marginal — between 1% and 50% within the relevant zone — so the on-field decision stands.
In an LBW review, the area of the stumps from their base to the top of the bails, between the outer edges of off and leg stump.
